text: **Work Summary – Sophie Bernard, AI Researcher**  During this reporting period, I focused on advancing robustness in large language models through adversarial training and interpretability. My primary achievement was leading the development of a new evaluation framework that quantifies model susceptibility to semantic perturbations, not just token-level noise. This framework, now internally named "SemShift," produced a 23% reduction in failure cases when applied to our flagship summarization model during stress testing.  I collaborated with the safety team to integrate gradient-based attribution methods into our debugging pipeline. This allowed us to trace hallucinated outputs back to specific training clusters, resulting in two targeted data-cleaning campaigns that improved factual consistency scores by 11 points on the FActScore benchmark. Additionally, I designed and ran a series of ablation studies on attention head pruning, which informed a 15% parameter reduction without performance loss, contributing to our inference cost optimization initiative.  I also mentored two junior researchers, guiding them on reproducible experiment design and statistical significance testing. Together, we published a technical report on the limitations of current perplexity metrics for detecting distributional shift, which has been circulated for internal peer review and is slated for external submission next quarter.  Challenges remain in cross-domain generalization, particularly for low-resource language subsets. I have initiated a collaborative project with the multilingual team to build a synthetic data generator that leverages structural linguistics rules, with a prototype expected by the next sprint. Time management was strained due to overlapping deadlines, but I prioritized tasks based on downstream impact.  Overall, I met all key performance indicators for this period, including model safety milestones and documentation completeness. I am eager to continue refining our evaluation suite and to present our findings at the upcoming internal research symposium. Centralized data silos create perverse incentives for surveillance and data hoarding.
